- When sentiment is consistently high (≥0.8) over recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast by 1–3% for next period.
- When sentiment is consistently low (≤0.4) or shows sharp decline, model often underestimates; increase forecast by 1–3% to account for potential rebound.
- After a price spike (forecast > true outcome by >5%), model frequently overcorrects in subsequent periods; apply a “lag correction” — reduce forecast by 2–5% in the next 2–3 periods.
- If true outcome shows strong mean reversion (e.g., 3+ consecutive days below 70), model often fails to recognize it; adjust forecast downward by 2–4% for next 3–5 periods.
- When sentiment history shows alternating highs/lows (e.g., 0.8 → 0.2 → 0.8), model tends to “stick” to recent trend; apply a “sentiment smoothing” rule — average sentiment over 3–5 periods to guide forecast adjustment.
- For 30-day horizon, model often overestimates early in the forecast window (first 5–7 days); apply a “first-period discount” — reduce forecast by 1–2% for first 5 days.
- If true outcome is significantly below historical mean (e.g., <65) and sentiment is neutral or negative, model often fails to recognize risk; add a “risk buffer” — reduce forecast by 3–5% for next 3–5 periods.
